c0006: Equivalent covers per day, year-1 average: about 107 dine-in (tables and the window counter), about 58 from take-out and pickup (36 orders) and about 30 from delivery marketplaces (19 orders), counting each order as 1.6 covers. A Friday or Saturday night runs well above the average and a Tuesday well below it (Kit estimate). Compare it with the foot traffic on your street on a Friday night and a Tuesday at lunch, and with the orders that fit in a peak hour
c0008: Per cover, EXCL. sales tax and tip: a dine-in guest spends about $15.00 (food $12.00 plus beverage $3.00); a take-out order averages $28.00 and a marketplace order $32.00 (the menu is about 15% higher there). At 1.6 covers per order, that is $17.50 and $20.00 per cover, and the weighted average of the three channels is $16.52; the example rounds it to $16.50 (Kit estimate). The "Menu price incl. sales tax (calculated)" row below shows the price with your local rate applied
c0010: 365 days minus Thanksgiving, Christmas Day, New Year's Day and 2 maintenance days for the hood and the fryers. The restaurant is open 7 days a week. It is the SAME figure for the P&L, the break-even, the scenarios and the staffing hours
c0012: Regulars and more pickup orders in year 2. It applies to covers at the same average check; staffing does NOT rise with this percentage: it comes from the "Staffing" tab
c0014: On year 2. Conservative: the ceiling is set by the two flat-tops, the 44 seats on Friday and Saturday nights and the orders that fit in a peak hour
c0022: Cost of goods sold on food sales: about 34%, on the prudent side. The theoretical cost per burger in the Smash Burger Patty, Fries & Costing Calculator comes out lower, but the real number is what you buy against what you sell: it also carries cook loss, buns and sauces thrown out at close, staff meals, comps, the chicken, the bacon, the shakes, the promotions on the delivery marketplaces and a beef price that keeps rising. The beef price is a Kit estimate. Measure your usage in the first quarter and change this cell
c0024: Beverage cost of about 20% of menu price (Kit estimate): fountain soft drinks, shakes and beer (beer is about 25% of beverage sales). Ask your distributor for the beer terms in writing: whether it lends you the tap system, the minimum volume and the discounts
c0026: Wrappers, burger boxes, fry cups, sauce cups, bags, cups, napkins and gloves for every order that leaves the restaurant, plus containers for leftovers. Local packaging ordinances vary (some cities charge for or ban single-use items): check yours before ordering
c0028: Sales through delivery marketplaces (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub) with their commission, as a share of total sales: about 19 orders a day. Pickup orders placed directly with you (phone, website or kiosk) pay no commission and do not go here: push them. A smash burger travels worse than it looks: the crust softens, so use vented containers for the fries and test before you go higher
c0042: About 1,700 sq ft (158 sq m) of second-generation restaurant space with a Type I hood route to the roof possible: an open kitchen with two flat-tops and fryers, an order counter with a self-order kiosk, 44 seats (tables and a window counter) and a to-go packing and driver pickup area by the door, in a neighborhood with nightlife or a campus area in a mid-size city (150,000 to 500,000 people), no key money: about $32 per sq ft a year (Kit estimate, editable). The weight of rent on sales is calculated by the workbook itself in the rent row of the "3-Year P&L"
c0046: Gas for the flat-tops and the fryers, electricity for the walk-in, the reach-ins and the hood with its makeup air, and water. The example uses $1,900 per month (Kit estimate). Ask the landlord for the space's utility history
c0048: General liability, product liability, liquor liability (beer), property and workers' comp: about $7,500 a year in the example (Kit estimate). Tell your insurance broker you run gas flat-tops and fryers: it changes the premium and the terms
c0057: Nominal annual rate (not APR). The example uses 10% on an SBA 7(a) loan, which you apply for through your lender (SBA Microloans go up to $50,000). Ask two lenders for offers before you set it; the flat-tops, fryers and refrigeration can also be leased: compare
c0061: Interest-only period in years. The example uses 0: principal is repaid from the start. If your lender gives you an interest-only period while you build out, enter it here and check the cash cushion of that year on the "Break-Even" tab
c0063: Three months of fixed costs: the cushion for the opening ramp-up, which with Month 1 in January runs from January to April, when the calendar is also at its slowest
c0072: Rate on alcohol served to go or by delivery. The example uses ONE sales tax rate (8%) for everything, so this cell equals the rate on sales; some states tax food to go or alcohol differently, so check yours. There is no credit for the tax you pay on purchases (see the recoverable input tax cell below)
c0079: Build-out and installations: order counter and open kitchen, electrical, gas, plumbing, HVAC, hood duct and exhaust, signage and facade. Ten years straight-line in the example: confirm the tax treatment with your CPA
c0081: Flat-tops, fryers, Type I hood, walk-in and reach-ins, beverage station, dish machine, smallwares, furniture and POS with kiosk: seven years straight-line in the example. Confirm the tax life with your CPA
c0088: Indoor seats: 44 in total, at tables and at a window counter. Someone who picks up an order or gets it delivered does not take a seat: that is why the seat turns in the row above come out higher than what your dining room really does
c0090: A new burger restaurant draws curious first-timers in its first month, but regulars and your ratings on the delivery apps take a quarter to build: Month 1 (January) brings in 75% of what it will bring in at month four. With 100% the ramp-up is removed
c0094: Two months of rent before opening: the build-out, the hood duct, the gas lines and the permits. If the lender funds the loan when construction starts, add the interest of those months, which this workbook does not count, and remember that any interest-only period starts at signing
c0096: Cushion on the build-out and installations of the space, which is where surprises show up (the hood route to the roof, the electrical service, the gas service, the grease interceptor). A lender will not finance a renovation without one
c0101: Payment terms with the beef, bun, fries and beverage suppliers: what they finance for you. Negotiate it in writing: if your beef supplier asks for weekly payment or COD, lower this figure
c0118: State / local minimum wage; this plan budgets at least $15 per hour for everyone. Enter the full-time annual floor of your state and city if it is higher than the federal one ($7.25 per hour). With 0 the status light compares only against the federal minimum
c0145: Architect, MEP and hood drawings, plan review (Food Code 8-201.11) and permit fees (Kit estimate). Ask your health department and your building department what they need before you sign the lease
c0148: Build-out of a second-generation restaurant space of 1,700 sq ft: order counter, open kitchen in view, finished kitchen, slip-resistant floors, restrooms (one ADA-accessible), ceilings and acoustic insulation, plus signage and facade. Kit estimate: get two quotes
c0150: Exhaust duct from the Type I hood to the roof, with makeup air (the hood itself is in its own row). Ask the fire marshal and the mechanical inspector in writing what your city requires. Installers rarely quote by the foot: ask for an offer with your plans
c0152: Electrical service and panel for the walk-in, the reach-ins, the shake machine, the kiosk and the makeup air, plus HVAC. Ask what service is available BEFORE you sign: a new service takes time
c0154: Plumbing, the gas lines for the flat-tops and the fryers by a licensed plumber or gas fitter with permit and inspection, and the grease interceptor, which the county sizes at plan review
c0156: The steel flat-top where each ball is smashed: two 48" gas flat-tops with a bun toaster, smash presses ($10.49-25.99 each) and burger scrapers. A 36" gas flat-top lists from $589 (Avantco) to $4,858 (Imperial, 1" plate) (webstaurantstore, Oct 2026); no price was read for the 48" size. Kit estimate
c0158: Three gas fryers with filtration: the third is for the breaded chicken, so the fries are not cross-contacted with wheat, egg and milk. Includes the fry station. Kit estimate (no price read): ask your equipment dealer for the data sheet
c0160: Type I hood with UL 300 fire suppression over the flat-tops and the fryers. Hood and duct cleaning follows NFPA 96. Kit estimate: ask the fire marshal what your city requires
c0162: The make-line unit, the refrigerated chef base under the flat-top to keep the balls at 41 °F (5 °C) or below during service, and the cheese and holding station. Kit estimate
c0164: Walk-in cooler (6×8 ft) for the beef, the buns, the sauces and the produce, plus reach-ins, the freezer for the fries and an ice machine, with cold holding at 41 °F (5 °C) or below. A 6×8 ft walk-in lists around $12,800 (webstaurantstore, Oct 2026)
c0166: Shake machine, blenders and the beverage station (fountain and beer). Kit estimate
c0170: Portion scale in oz, ball portioner, thin-tip probe thermometers, a TPM tester or test strips, labels and the to-go station. Your written food safety plan can choose strips over a tester
c0172: Tables, chairs and stools for 44 seats, including the window counter, and the order counter
c0174: POS with a self-order kiosk, a kitchen display (KDS), online ordering and the tablets for the delivery marketplaces
c0176: LLC formation (ask your CPA about LLC vs S corp), EIN and state payroll registration, business license and sales tax permit, building permit and certificate of occupancy, health permit with plan review, the written food safety plan and two weeks of pre-opening training. Fees vary by city: replace this line with your own quotes
c0179: Branding, a website with the menu and the allergens, a photo session and the launch video (a smash burger sells on video)
c0181: Beef (bought already ground or in balls, with the supplier's establishment number), potato buns, American cheese, frozen fries, oil, sauces, the first order of to-go packaging and the beverages
c0215: Burgers, chicken sandwich, fries and sides: about 50% of sales dine-in, 31% take-out and 19% through delivery marketplaces. One sales tax rate in the example, whether it is eaten at the restaurant or taken away
c0241: Hood and duct cleaning every quarter (NFPA 96: ask your fire marshal), service of the flat-tops and the gas lines, the fryers, and the refrigeration technician for the walk-in, the reach-ins and the freezer
c0243: Google Business Profile, Yelp, Instagram and TikTok video (a smash burger sells on video), photos, the delivery marketplaces' promotions and the peak dates (National Burger Month in May, Super Bowl Sunday, March Madness); the opening campaign is in startup costs
c0245: POS subscription (a POS that reports sales tax), self-order kiosk and online ordering, the delivery tablets, phone and internet
c0249: Trash and cardboard pickup, the grease interceptor service and the used fryer oil, collected by a licensed renderer: never down the drain or back into the kitchen. Enter the rates of your city
c0255: Certified Food Protection Manager (CFPM) and food handler cards, ground beef and fryer safety training, allergen training, and OSHA basics: flat-top and fryer burns, cuts, slips on grease and lifting
c0279: Floor for the margin after ALL variable costs (food and beverage, disposables, marketplace fees, card fees and miscellaneous). With about 19% of sales through marketplaces, a burger restaurant leaves less than a dining room alone: if marketplaces grow, this margin drops. Kit estimate
c0282: Ceiling for cost of goods sold on sales: beef is more than half of the food purchases and its price rules. Kit estimate
c0284: Ceiling for labor on sales with counter service, two flat-tops and seven days a week. No servers and no tips modeled. Kit estimate
c0288: Floor for the net result on sales at full pace so the plan holds up. Kit estimate
c0322: Full services per seat per day you can run over 11 open hours, with orders placed at the counter and stays of 20-30 minutes. It is the physical ceiling of the space, not a target. The dining room alone gives about 2.4; cash break-even needs fewer (row 26)
c0363: Buys the beef and picks the blend (chuck, brisket, short rib) and the suppliers, signs off the menu, runs the marketplaces and manages, and covers the rush on the line. About $4,500 per month in the example. The workbook imputes a monthly salary as if on payroll, which is the prudent side; confirm with your CPA how you will pay yourself (owner's draw or W-2 under an S corp). The example pays the owner below a chain manager: owner's draw in addition from net profit
c0365: Two grill cooks run the smash station on the flat-top: the smash, the crust, the timing and the probe check on one burger per batch. About $17 per hour in the example (the BLS median for restaurant cooks is about $17.98). With a single grill cook, one absence closes the line
c0367: The fryers, the fries, the nightly oil filtering, the sauces, the portioned balls and the mise en place: about $16 per hour in the example
c0369: Opens or closes, runs the register, the kiosk and the marketplace tablets, keeps the temperature log and answers allergen questions: about $21 per hour in the example
c0371: Cashier, expo and to-go packing: three people at 0.75 each, about $15.50 per hour. No tips are modeled: the tip jar belongs to the team
c0373: Part-time W-2 crew for Friday to Sunday: the second flat-top and the packing. About $15.50 per hour, never as a 1099 contractor. This plan has NO in-house delivery: if you add it, the driver is a W-2 employee with hired and non-owned auto insurance
c0389: Hours the restaurant is open to the public, 7 days a week: 11:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m., and until 11:00 p.m. on Friday and Saturday. There is no afternoon close
c0391: Average number of people at the same time across the flat-top, the fryer, the counter and the expo. On Friday and Saturday nights you need more: the weekend crew comes in (the annual roster does not see them: put them in the shift)
c0393: The day's portioned balls, cuts, sauces and restocking the line before opening, from 8:30 a.m.
c0395: A grill cook and the fry & prep cook. Closing, cleaning the flat-tops and the fryers, and purchasing are outside this schedule: they are the margin between the hours you hire and the hours you need
c0411: 4. All figures are EXCL. SALES TAX. To turn a menu price into a price excl. sales tax, divide it by 1 plus your sales tax rate (a rate of 8% means dividing by 1.08). The example uses ONE rate for everything: dine-in, take-out, delivery and beverages; some states tax food to go or alcohol differently, so check yours. The P&L is excl. sales tax; the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab shows what you actually collect, sales tax included, and the sales tax you remit as a quarterly filer.
c0413: 6. The "12-Month Cash Flow" tab answers the question that decides a bank deal: in which month the cash runs out. Its Month 1 is JANUARY, in calendar order: the opening ramp-up runs from January to April, and January is also one of the slow months of the calendar, which is why working capital counts. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row. The minimum balance of the year can never come out in red.
c0415: 8. The Word business plan in this kit quotes the figures in this Excel: if you change a green cell, the Excel rules. The Smash Burger Patty, Fries & Costing Calculator is separate: it works out the cost of the beef, the balls and patties that come out of each pound, the cost of each portion of fries and the oil, and it COSTS each burger and combo by channel. Do not copy the food cost of one burger into the "0. Assumptions" tab: the "Cost of goods sold on FOOD sales" cell is the weighted average of the WHOLE menu plus the buns and sauces thrown out at close, staff meals and marketplace promotions, and that is why it comes out higher than the theoretical cost per burger. With the costing of your own menu, check that this average holds.
c0436: In calendar order: the ramp-up falls on January to April. February is the slowest month, with January and November behind it. May (National Burger Month and graduations), June, July and August are the peaks. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row of the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab
